Summary: 
The Bank of Korea’s 2024 forecast warns that South Korea’s record‑low birth rate of 0.748 (up from 0.721 in 2023) could trigger a prolonged economic downturn by the 2040s. Seoul has spent over $270 billion in 16 years on incentives such as baby bonuses and cash rewards, and in 2023 proposed exempting men with three or more children from mandatory military service. The pension system is also under strain; a March reform extends the depletion of the state pension fund by 15 years to 2071, and the military and civil‑servant pensions are already depleted. Active troops have fallen 20 % to about 450,000 from 690,000 in 2019, while North Korea maintains a 1.23 million‑strong force. Despite the bleak outlook, Lee, former director general of the national statistics agency, cautioned that economies can adapt through technology, immigration and other measures, saying, 'When an economy faces recession, it typically responds with various efforts to enhance productivity through technological innovation, immigration policies, and other measures to prevent further decline.' Eberstadt echoed this optimism, pointing to the 1970s fears of resource scarcity and concluding, 'Human beings are a uniquely adaptable,' and that the record of the immediate past does not warrant betting against South Korea’s future prosperity.

The current fertility rate means only about 36 children per 100 people, far below the OECD average of 1.43 and the replacement level of 2.1. Lee In‑sil, Director of the Korea Peninsula Population Institute for Future, told CNBC that without technological innovation the country will face a "sustained economic slowdown". Seoul has spent over $270 billion in 16 years on incentives such as baby bonuses and cash rewards, and in 2023 proposed exempting men with three or more children from mandatory military service. Yet Nicholas Eberstadt of the American Enterprise Institute said, 'I don't think there's any way that population policy can effectively raise fertility levels in South Korea in any appreciable way,' and noted the TFR remains far below 2.1. The pension system is also under strain; a March reform extends the depletion of the state pension fund by 15 years to 2071, and the military and civil‑servant pensions are already depleted. Active troops have fallen 20 % to about 450,000 from 690,000 in 2019, while North Korea maintains a 1.23 million‑strong force. Despite the bleak outlook, Lee, former director general of the national statistics agency, cautioned that economies can adapt through technology, immigration and other measures, saying, 'When an economy faces recession, it typically responds with various efforts to enhance productivity through technological innovation, immigration policies, and other measures to prevent further decline.' Eberstadt echoed this optimism, pointing to the 1970s fears of resource scarcity and concluding, 'Human beings are a uniquely adaptable,' and that the record of the immediate past does not warrant betting against South Korea’s future prosperity.
